content: Mometasone furoate is practically insoluble in water. It exhibits slight solubility in methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol, while being soluble in acetone and chloroform. It is freely soluble in tetrahydrofuran. The partition coefficient of mometasone furoate between octanol and water is greater than 5000. A formulation containing 0.05% w/w mometasone furoate (calculated on an anhydrous basis) is prepared in an aqueous medium that includes glycerin, microcrystalline cellulose, carboxymethylcellulose sodium, sodium citrate, citric acid, benzalkonium chloride, and polysorbate 80. Pharmacodynamics Adrenal Function in Adults: Four clinical pharmacology studies have been conducted to evaluate the effects of mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) on adrenal function at various doses. 1. Study 1: In a study involving 64 patients (aged 22 to 44 years) with allergic rhinitis, daily doses of 200 mcg and 400 mcg of mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) were compared to 10 mg of prednisone and placebo over 36 consecutive days. Adrenal function was assessed by measuring plasma cortisol levels after a 6-hour ACTH (Cortrosyn) infusion and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels. Mometasone nasal spray at both 200 mcg and 400 mcg doses did not result in statistically significant decreases in mean plasma cortisol levels post-Cortrosyn infusion or in 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. In contrast, the prednisone group showed statistically significant decreases in both plasma cortisol levels and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. 2. Study 2: This study evaluated adrenal response in 48 male volunteers (aged 21 to 40 years) treated with mometasone nasal spray (400 mcg and 1600 mcg/day), prednisone (10 mg/day), or placebo for 29 days. Adrenal function was assessed by measuring the 24-hour plasma cortisol area under the curve (AUC0–24), plasma cortisol levels during and after an 8-hour ACTH infusion, and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels. No statistically significant differences in adrenal function were observed with mometasone nasal spray compared to placebo. 3. Study 3: In a study involving 24 male volunteers (aged 22 to 39 years), single rising doses of mometasone nasal spray (1000, 2000, and 4000 mcg/day), orally administered mometasone furoate (2000, 4000, and 8000 mcg/day), orally administered dexamethasone (200, 400, and 800 mcg/day), and placebo were evaluated. Dose administrations were separated by at least 72 hours. Plasma cortisol levels at 8 AM and over a 24-hour period were measured to calculate the plasma cortisol AUC0–24. Additionally, 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were collected. No statistically significant decreases in plasma cortisol AUC, 8 AM cortisol levels, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were observed in volunteers treated with mometasone nasal spray or oral mometasone compared to placebo. Conversely, nearly all volunteers treated with dexamethasone exhibited abnormal 8 AM cortisol levels (<10 mcg/dL), reduced 24-hour plasma AUC values, and decreased 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. 4. Study 4: Adrenal function was assessed in 213 patients (aged 18 to 81 years) with nasal polyps before and after 4 months of treatment with mometasone nasal spray (200 mcg once or twice daily) or placebo by measuring 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels. Mometasone nasal spray at both doses (200 and 400 mcg/day) was not associated with statistically significant decreases in 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. Pharmacodynamics Adrenal Function in Pediatric Patients: Three clinical pharmacology studies were conducted to evaluate the effects of mometasone furoate nasal spray on adrenal function in pediatric patients at daily doses of 50, 100, and 200 mcg compared to placebo. 1. Study 1: In a study involving 48 pediatric patients (aged 6 to 11 years) with allergic rhinitis, adrenal function was assessed before and after 7 consecutive days of treatment by measuring morning plasma cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels. Mometasone furoate nasal spray at all three doses was not associated with statistically significant decreases in mean plasma cortisol levels or 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. 2. Study 2: In a study involving 48 pediatric patients (aged 3 to 5 years) with allergic rhinitis, adrenal function was assessed before and after 14 consecutive days of treatment by measuring plasma cortisol levels following a 30-minute ACTH (Cortrosyn) infusion. Mometasone furoate nasal spray (50 mcg) at all three doses (50, 100, and 200 mcg/day) was not associated with statistically significant decreases in mean plasma cortisol levels post-Cortrosyn infusion compared to placebo. All patients demonstrated a normal response to Cortrosyn. 3. Study 3: In a study involving 52 pediatric patients (aged 2 to 5 years) with allergic rhinitis, adrenal function was assessed before and after up to 42 consecutive days of once-daily treatment. Twenty-eight patients received mometasone furoate nasal spray (50 mcg per nostril, total daily dose 100 mcg). Morning plasma cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were measured. Mometasone furoate nasal spray was not associated with statistically significant decreases in mean plasma cortisol levels or 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. Distribution: In vitro studies indicate that mometasone furoate exhibits a protein binding rate of 98% to 99% within a concentration range of 5 to 500 ng/mL. Metabolism: Studies have demonstrated that any portion of a mometasone furoate dose that is swallowed and absorbed undergoes extensive metabolism, resulting in the formation of multiple metabolites.
